settings.content: How to work out what they actually want, without asking

settings.heading: Their Taste Is the Only One That Matters
settings.body:
The ring is for the person who will wear it every day for decades. Their taste is the only one that counts, and the single most common regret we hear is from people who chose what they liked rather than what their partner would have chosen.

The good news is that most people broadcast their taste constantly without realising. You do not need to ask, and you do not need to guess. You need to look properly at what is already there.

settings.heading: Observe their jewellery
settings.body: Gold, silver or rose-toned? Minimal and modern, or ornate and vintage? Delicate pieces or bolder statements? Slim bands or chunkier designs? Their existing jewellery tells you more than any questionnaire could.

settings.heading: Consider their wider aesthetic
settings.body: Their wardrobe, their home, their saved images, the people whose style they admire. Tailored neutrals suggest a different ring from flowing florals and antiques.

settings.heading: Lifestyle matters
settings.body: Are they hands-on at work or in their hobbies? A raised, delicate setting will snag with heavy use, while a low-profile bezel wears beautifully through an active life.

settings.heading: Enlist help
settings.body: Their closest friend, sibling or parent almost always has a clearer picture than has ever been said out loud. And if they have shown you a ring they love, take it entirely seriously.

settings.heading: Metal tone is the strongest signal
settings.body: Almost nobody wears white and yellow metal interchangeably. Look at what is actually on them day to day, not what is in the jewellery box. If everything is warm-toned, a platinum ring will feel like someone else's.

settings.heading: Scale tells you more than shape
settings.body: Someone who wears fine chains and small studs will find a large centre stone uncomfortable in a way that has nothing to do with taste. Someone who wears bold pieces will find a delicate ring disappears on them.

settings.heading: Watch what they never wear
settings.body: The pieces sitting untouched in the box are as informative as the ones in daily rotation. There is usually a reason, and it is often comfort rather than looks.

settings.heading: Vintage or modern is a real divide
settings.body: People rarely sit in the middle. Milgrain, filigree and cluster designs speak to one sensibility; clean bezels and solitaires to another. Getting this wrong is more noticeable than getting the stone wrong.

settings.heading: Ask about other people's rings
settings.body: A friend's engagement is the most natural possible opening. What they say about someone else's ring is usually a direct statement about their own preferences.

settings.heading: Take photographs
settings.body: Of their hand, of jewellery they wear, of anything they have pointed at. Send them to us. We can read a great deal from a few images that is difficult to put into words.

settings.heading: Choosing for Yourself, Not for Them
settings.body:
After years of these conversations, this is the regret that surfaces most often. It rarely looks like a mistake at the time: you choose the ring you find most beautiful, and it is beautiful. It is simply not theirs.

If you are torn between what you love and what they would choose, choose theirs. And if choosing is paralysing you entirely, propose with a temporary band and design the real ring together afterwards. We do this routinely and credit the placeholder against the final piece.

settings.cells: Hands-on or active | Bezel, low-profile solitaire, flush-set | Secure and snag-free above all
Desk-based or creative | Almost anything | Pavé, halo and three-stone all wear well
Hands in water often | Bezel or low-profile platinum | Avoid softer stones entirely
Vintage lovers | Cluster, milgrain, filigree, hidden halo | Detail rewards close looking
Minimalists | Solitaire, east-west, bezel | A plain band with a stand-out stone

settings.heading: Style by Lifestyle
settings.intro: Taste tells you what they would choose. Lifestyle tells you what will still look good in ten years.

settings.q: How do I find out what ring they want without giving it away?
settings.a: Look at the jewellery they already wear, particularly the metal tone and the scale. Ask what they think of a friend's ring. Involve their closest friend or sibling, who almost always knows. Photographs of their hand and their existing pieces tell us a great deal.

settings.q: What if I get it wrong?
settings.a: The surest way to avoid it is to propose with a temporary ring, then design the real one together. If a finished ring is not loved, we will advise on reselling and help you redesign and remake it at cost price.
Yes, but keep the circle small. Engagement ring conversations travel fast, and telling several people before your partner knows is one of the most common ways a surprise is spoiled.

settings.q: They wear both gold and silver. What do I do?
settings.a: Look at what is on them right now rather than what they own. Most people who claim to wear both have a clear daily default. If they genuinely alternate, a two-tone design or a white metal setting on a yellow band solves it.

settings.q: Can I send you photographs and let you advise?
settings.a: Please do, it is the fastest route to the right ring. Send images of jewellery they already wear, anything they have pointed at, their rough finger size, your budget and your timeline. We never share details with anyone but you.
